appraisal_events.evidence: « il faudrait au moins raconter la vérité et ne pas en manger la moitié »; « il faut du reste reconnaître que tous ces gens ont été fort polis »; « un membre du tribunal révolutionnaire qui a fait périr en un jour onze des nôtres »
appraisal_events.explanation: Distinct from the duchess's diminishment, the duke himself is given the last, extended word: he corrects the record, shows measured fairness toward political adversaries, and invokes his family's long, tragic aristocratic lineage, positioning him as the more authoritative and dignified speaker in this exchange.

appraisal_events.evidence: « mon petit Swann... vous n'avez pas envoyé la photographie de nos chevaliers de Rhodes, que j'aime par vous et avec qui j'ai si envie de faire connaissance »
appraisal_events.explanation: The duchess addresses Swann with familiar affection and expressed desire for something only he can provide, marking him as a valued intimate, though the address is also used strategically to change an awkward subject, making the sincerity of the warmth somewhat uncertain.

status_effects.explanation: He holds the floor with a long, judicious, corrective account, ending the exchange as the authoritative voice on the family's history.
The duchess singles him out with familiar, affectionate address and an expressed wish to be closer to him, signaling his valued place in her circle.

ambiguities: Legrandin and M. Vinteuil are named only inside a retrospective analogy about past instances of social insincerity (parents discussing 'corruption' with Vinteuil, Legrandin softening his diction for people he privately scorned); this is backward-looking commentary rather than a local event of the present scene, so they were not scored.

Swann's warm address from the duchess ('mon petit Swann') doubles as a deliberate change of subject away from her husband's anger, so it is unclear whether the affection is genuine esteem or purely instrumental politeness.
